project: WO-C2 Correction 2 — Make Work Watch Survive Model-Response Retry Collisions
description: Make finite and --follow Work watch streams survive live-shaped model-response retry collisions, prevent new model-response identity collisions, and prove the behavior with a complete recorded production ledger while preserving corruption detection and the existing NDJSON contract.

context.customerAsk: Make you work watch stream real production sessions end-to-end despite repeated model-response IDs, extend the accepted retry/replay semantics from #1833 beyond MODEL_REQUEST, audit and correct the response ID construction that embeds model-request/1, retain same-sequence corruption rejection, and add complete production-ledger functional coverage for finite and --follow modes.
context.problem: The watch reducer treats a later model-response record that reuses a request-ordinal-derived event ID as conflicting canonical data and aborts. The #1833 exception covers only MODEL_REQUEST, model-response IDs can collide across dispatch retries, and synthetic fixtures have twice failed to reproduce the full live event mix.
context.solution: Use one sequence-aware policy for every non-projecting enrichment family: exact replay is idempotent, refreshed same-ID data is accepted only at a strictly later sequence, and conflicting same or backward sequence reuse remains an error. Give newly recorded retry responses distinct stable event IDs while preserving request correlation, then verify finite and follow behavior through the application watch pipeline using a complete redacted production ledger.

acceptanceCriteria: Finite you work watch --session <session> replays the complete production-ledger fixture through terminal Work state and exits successfully without aborting on the observed model-response ID family.

you work watch --session <session> --follow consumes the same retained production history, remains attached after terminal history, emits later Work transitions once each, and stops cleanly only when canceled by the test.

Repeated non-projecting enrichment events with refreshed canonical data are accepted only at strictly increasing sequences, while conflicting reuse at the same or a lower sequence fails and leaves the last accepted cursor unchanged.
Newly recorded model responses for distinct retry executions cannot reuse a canonical event ID; exact replay of one recorded event retains its original identity and request correlation.
No storage engine is added, no you.work.watch.v1 NDJSON field or shape changes, and the cut list in docs/temp/work-order.md remains out of scope.

The named regression command go test ./pkg/services/work/transports/cli ./pkg/services/workers/internal/services/workstations/execution/recording ./tests/functional/work/watch -count=1 and make verify-fast pass; Typecheck passes; Tests pass; no NEW lint violations relative to current main, and the gates green on main (backend-size, pkg-maint, pkg-file-count, pkg-structure, vet) stay green.

The implementation/review loop continues until required CI is terminal and passing, all blocking PR conversation feedback is explicitly addressed, merge conflicts and shared-file changes are reconciled, and the PR is actually merged.

userStories.title: Accept ordered enrichment retries without hiding corruption
userStories.description: As an operator watching Work, I want repeated model-response and equivalent enrichment records at later canonical positions to be treated as retry history so that unrelated enrichment cannot abort the Work transition stream.
acceptanceCriteria: The exact live-shaped ID factory-event/model-response/2cf2a099-909b-4446-8e8d-1453054e093c/model-request/1 can recur with refreshed model-response canonical data at a strictly later sequence without emitting a Work line or returning an error.
The same sequence-aware behavior covers every non-projecting enrichment event family accepted by the watch reducer, with no event-family-specific retry exception left as the policy boundary.
Exact replays remain idempotent, advance neither emitted output nor cursor, and do not duplicate Work transitions.
A same-ID event with conflicting canonical data at the same or a lower sequence is rejected, and the cursor remains at the last valid event.
Finite and follow stream tests prove that valid Work transitions before, between, and after refreshed enrichment events are emitted once in strictly increasing sequence order.
Tests pass
Typecheck passes
userStories.notes: Generalized watch ordering so every currently defined non-projecting Factory event family uses the same ordered-enrichment policy: exact replay is idempotent, refreshed same-ID data is accepted only at a strictly later canonical sequence, and same/backward conflicting reuse is rejected without moving the cursor. Added reducer coverage for the complete current non-projecting event vocabulary, including the live-shaped model-response ID factory-event/model-response/2cf2a099-909b-4446-8e8d-1453054e093c/model-request/1, plus finite and --follow model-response retry streams. The focused regression command and make verify-fast pass.

userStories.title: Give distinct model responses collision-safe event identities
userStories.description: As a maintainer of the canonical Factory ledger, I want distinct response records from dispatch retries to have distinct event identities so that new recordings do not manufacture ambiguous replay keys.
acceptanceCriteria: Two distinct model-response records produced for retry executions within the same dispatch lifecycle receive different canonical event IDs, even when both correlate to request ordinal model-request/1.
A response event retains explicit correlation to its matching model request, and request/response payload meaning is unchanged.
Reconstructing or replaying the same response record preserves its event ID; identity generation does not depend on wall-clock coincidence or mutable payload serialization.
Focused recording tests cover successful and failed responses across retries and demonstrate the no-collision invariant.
No Factory Event payload schema or Work-watch NDJSON shape changes.
Tests pass
Typecheck passes
userStories.notes: Added a deterministic response ordinal per dispatch lifecycle and used it for model-response event IDs, while preserving the existing model-request/1 retry correlation and all response payload fields. The ordinal remains independent of wall-clock time and mutable payload data, so the event ID is stable when the recorded response is replayed. Added focused recorder coverage for failed-then-successful retries, distinct response IDs, unchanged request correlation, and deterministic identity generation. The focused regression command passes. No Factory Event payload schema or Work-watch NDJSON changes were made.

userStories.title: Replay a complete production retry ledger through Work watch
userStories.description: As an operator, I want the watch command verified against the full event mix from a real retried session so that synthetic coverage cannot mask another live-stream abort.
acceptanceCriteria: A complete recorded production ledger from a real session with dispatch retries is checked in as a stable, secret-free fixture; redaction preserves event order, event families, sequence values, repeated-ID relationships, Work lineage, and terminal outcome needed by the regression.
The fixture contains the observed model-response request-ordinal ID shape and at least one refreshed occurrence at a later canonical sequence.
An application-level functional test routes the recorded ledger through the same service and CLI watch pipeline used by Process.Execute, rather than invoking the reducer alone or a built you binary.
Finite mode emits only the expected you.work.watch.v1 Work transitions in canonical order, reaches the recorded terminal cohort, and exits successfully with no stderr error.

Follow mode drains the same retained ledger without duplicates or collision errors, remains subscribed, emits a deterministically supplied later Work transition once, and exits cleanly on cancellation without sleeps as synchronization.
The functional scenario rejects a deliberately same-sequence conflicting event derived from the fixture, proving that production compatibility does not weaken corruption detection.
